abstract: We present OmniVoice, a massively multilingual zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) model that scales to over 600 languages. At its core is a novel diffusion language model-style discrete non-autoregressive (NAR) architecture. Unlike conventional discrete NAR models that suffer from performance bottlenecks in complex two-stage (text-to-semantic-to-acoustic) pipelines, OmniVoice directly maps text to multi-codebook acoustic tokens. This simplified approach is facilitated by two key technical innovations: (1) a full-codebook random masking strategy for efficient training, and (2) initialization from a pre-trained LLM to ensure superior intelligibility. By leveraging a 581k-hour multilingual dataset curated entirely from open-source data, OmniVoice achieves the broadest language coverage to date and delivers state-of-the-art performance across Chinese, English, and diverse multilingual benchmarks. Our code and pre-trained models are publicly available.

sections.body: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) models cover only a few languages, and two-stage discrete non-autoregressive (NAR) systems pass errors from a semantic stage into the audio and lose acoustic detail. OmniVoice uses a single-stage discrete NAR model. It applies a discrete masked diffusion objective with a bidirectional Transformer to map text directly to multi-codebook acoustic tokens. Two changes make this work: full-codebook random masking for training efficiency, and initialization from pre-trained autoregressive (AR) LLM weights for intelligibility. The model is trained on a 581k-hour open-source multilingual dataset. The authors report experiments on Chinese, English and multilingual benchmarks covering up to 102 languages, and they claim leading results on intelligibility, speaker similarity and naturalness.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing zero-shot speech models cover few languages, and two-stage discrete pipelines suffer error propagation and information bottlenecks.

sections.body: The model takes a text token sequence and a multi-codebook acoustic matrix in which a prompt segment is kept and target tokens are replaced by a mask token. Each codebook has its own embedding layer and prediction head. For each training instance a masking ratio $p_t$ is drawn from a uniform distribution, and every entry of the time-by-codebook matrix is masked independently. The text states that on average 50% of tokens enter the loss, $C$ times more than per-layer masking. LLM initialization transfers pre-trained weights to a backbone with the same structure, and the authors report that causal-trained weights work in the bidirectional model. Low-resource languages are upsampled with beta set to 0.8. Controls cover prompt denoising, speaker-attribute voice design, paralinguistic cues and phonetic overrides.
sections.heading: Proposed Method
sections.headline: Full-codebook random masking and LLM initialization form the method, trained on more than 600 languages from 581k hours of audio.

sections.body: Two training variants are described. A bilingual variant uses the Chinese and English subsets of Emilia with prompt denoising omitted. A multilingual variant uses the 581k-hour dataset. The backbone is initialized from Qwen3-0.6B weights, and the Higgs-audio tokenizer provides 8-codebook acoustic tokens. Training uses the AdamW optimizer with a peak learning rate of 1e-4 on 8 H800 GPUs. The multilingual variant ran 2M updates in 9.66 days. Inference uses 32 unmasking steps. Benchmarks are LibriSpeech-PC test-clean, Seed-TTS, MiniMax-Multilingual-24 and FLEURS-Multilingual-102. Metrics are speaker similarity (SIM-o), word or character error rate, UTMOS, and subjective CMOS and SMOS scores.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Models are compared on Chinese, English and multilingual benchmarks using speaker similarity, error rates and subjective listening scores.

sections.body: On LibriSpeech-PC test-clean, OmniVoice reports speaker similarity of 0.729, word error rate (WER) of 1.30 and UTMOS of 4.28. On Seed-TTS, it reports SIM-o of 0.741 for English and 0.777 for Chinese, with WER of 1.60 and 0.84. Qwen3-TTS has a higher LibriSpeech-PC UTMOS of 4.41. OmniVoice-Emilia, trained on the same data as the NAR baselines, outperforms F5-TTS, ZipVoice and MaskGCT. In subjective tests, OmniVoice reports CMOS of 0.44 and SMOS of 3.80. On MiniMax-Multilingual-24, Table 3 gives a Chinese WER of 1.008 for OmniVoice, against 2.252 for MiniMax and 16.026 for ElevenLabs. Some languages in that table still show higher WER for OmniVoice than for a baseline.
sections.heading: Experimental Results
sections.headline: OmniVoice gets the lowest word error rate on LibriSpeech-PC test-clean, at 1.30, and the highest subjective similarity score, at 3.80, among compared models.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that OmniVoice supports more than 600 languages through a single-stage discrete NAR framework that maps text to multi-codebook acoustic tokens. It credits full-codebook random masking with training efficiency and LLM weight initialization with intelligibility. The authors state that the model has the broadest zero-shot language coverage reported to date. They also describe it as equipped with high inference efficiency, and present the work as an advance toward high-quality speech across many of the world's languages.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: The authors conclude that the single-stage design, masking and LLM initialization together give broad language coverage and efficient inference.

sections.body: Appendix A lists the datasets used for training, including Emilia, Common Voice, FLEURS and many regional corpora. Appendix B reports English and Chinese results at 64, 32, 16 and 8 inference steps, with a WER of 1.50 on LibriSpeech-PC test-clean at 16 steps. Appendix C gives per-language character error rates for ground truth and OmniVoice on FLEURS-Multilingual-102. Appendix D lists 646 supported languages with 581k hours of training data. Appendix E states limitations: uneven annotation and acoustic quality in open-source sources, limited instruction-tuning data, no optimization for complex numeric sequences, and no existing inference acceleration for discrete NAR models. Appendix F states ethics and misuse risks.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists training datasets, inference-step and per-language results, supported languages, limitations and ethics statements.
